# The Map {#sec-map .unnumbered}

A model learns the distribution it is trained on, through the representation it is given. This
page sets out the lens the book uses to read every data technique, the questions the book
answers and where, and three ways through it.

## Four levers, and evaluation

Every technique that acts on training data changes one or more of four things:

- **The representation:** how inputs and targets are encoded and transformed. Scaling, log
  transforms, encodings, spectrograms and imputation pull this lever. It changes what the model
  can see and, for the target, what the loss averages
  ([Changing the Shape](06-changing-the-shape.qmd#sec-shape)).
- **The sampling distribution $q$:** which examples are drawn, compared with the target
  distribution $p$ the model will face. Stratification, resampling, augmentation,
  deduplication and data selection pull this lever
  ([The Data-Generating Process](01-the-data-generating-process.qmd#sec-dgp)).
- **The weights $w$:** how much each example counts. Class weights, prior-shift correction and
  importance weights pull this lever. Resampling and reweighting aim at the same target, the
  distribution proportional to $q \cdot w$; they differ in variance
  ([Sampling and Weighting](08-sampling-and-weighting.qmd#sec-sampling)).
- **The labels:** what each example says. Label noise, label correction and label-changing
  augmentation act here ([Labels](02-labels.qmd#sec-labels)).

Some techniques change none of the four. Splits, leakage control, deduplication across a
split, shift detection and learning-curve estimation change what is *measured*, not what is
learned. Their cards say *evaluation only*.

Which lever a technique pulls decides what it can fix and what it can break. A representation
cannot correct a biased sample; a weight cannot add an input the model never sees; a relabeling
cannot remove a shift in the inputs. Every technique gets a **data card** that names its lever,
the assumption it rests on, what it does to the learned function, what it is fit on, how it
fails and which test checks it.

{{< include ../includes/cards/log-target.md >}}

The pair $(q, w)$ is the pair `rl-for-llms` uses to describe reinforcement-learning methods
for language models, where $q$ is the data regime and $w$ the per-sample weight of the
estimator ([rl-for-llms, The Map](https://ioannisantoniadis.github.io/rl-for-llms/chapters/00-map.html)).
Here it describes data engineering.

## The questions, and where they are answered

| Question | Short answer | Where |
|---|---|---|
| When should a log transform replace standard or min-max scaling, and which models care? | Affine scaling never changes a distribution's shape; it matters to distance-based, regularized and gradient-trained models, and not to tree splits. A nonlinear transform changes the shape and, for a target, what the loss estimates | [Affine Scaling](05-affine-scaling.qmd#sec-affine), [Changing the Shape](06-changing-the-shape.qmd#sec-shape) |
| What do text, images, audio and tables each require? | A representation that exposes their structure: frequencies for audio, order for time series, codes for categories, counts for text | [Data Types](03-data-types.qmd#sec-data-types), [Encoding and Features](07-encoding-and-features.qmd#sec-encoding) |
| When to resample and when to reweight? | Both aim at the same target; reweighting keeps all the data and has lower variance; both need a probability correction afterwards | [Sampling and Weighting](08-sampling-and-weighting.qmd#sec-sampling) |
| What does augmentation actually add? | An assumption about $p$: helpful when the invariance is true, label noise when it is not | [Augmentation](09-augmentation.qmd#sec-augmentation) |
| How much data does a problem need, and what does that depend on? | Noise sets the floor, dimension and target complexity the approach; a pilot can bound the error but rarely the data needed near the floor | [Learning Curves](11-learning-curves.qmd#sec-learning-curves) |
| Why do returns on more data diminish as a power law? | Several accounts; in one, made exact here, error is the probability mass of cases not yet seen, which falls as a power law when cases are long-tailed | [Scaling Laws](12-scaling-laws.qmd#sec-scaling-laws), [Why Power Laws](13-why-power-laws.qmd#sec-long-tail) |
| Can smarter selection beat that law? | Not escape it. Per label, skipping what is already covered steepens it; per example drawn, nothing does better; practical selectors each work under a condition | [Why Power Laws](13-why-power-laws.qmd#sec-long-tail), [Choosing Data](14-choosing-data.qmd#sec-choosing-data) |

The last row differs from the question as first posed: the book set out to show how selection
can beat the power law, and the exact model showed that it cannot, only steepen it per label.

## How the book argues

Every chapter follows the same template: the problem, the assumptions, a derivation or a
demonstration, a boxed result, what it does to the learned model, its failure modes with a
figure, what the toy cannot show, and connections.

- **Computed, not illustrated.** Every figure is produced by a script from one of five
  synthetic testbeds whose truth is known exactly
  ([The Testbeds](../appendix-testbeds.qmd#sec-testbeds)). Every checkable statement names
  the test that checks it. From [Sampling and Weighting](08-sampling-and-weighting.qmd#sec-sampling) on, every quoted number is written into the text by the script that computed it; earlier numbers were copied from fresh runs and rechecked.
- **Evidence labeled.** Statements about the literature carry their status: a mathematical
  fact, a replicated finding, a single study, or contested, with a date where the field is
  moving.
- **Limits stated.** Each chapter says what its toy cannot show; the list is collected in
  [What the Toys Cannot Show](../appendix-toy-limits.qmd#sec-toy-limits).

## Reading paths

- **Preparing a dataset for a model:** [The Data-Generating Process](01-the-data-generating-process.qmd#sec-dgp),
  then [Cleaning](04-cleaning.qmd#sec-cleaning) to
  [Encoding and Features](07-encoding-and-features.qmd#sec-encoding),
  [Sampling and Weighting](08-sampling-and-weighting.qmd#sec-sampling), and
  [A Data Decision Guide](15-decision-guide.qmd#sec-decision-guide).
- **Deciding how much data to collect, and which:**
  [Learning Curves](11-learning-curves.qmd#sec-learning-curves) through
  [Choosing Data](14-choosing-data.qmd#sec-choosing-data).
- **Deployment data that will not look like the training data:**
  [Distribution Shift](10-distribution-shift.qmd#sec-shift),
  [Sampling and Weighting](08-sampling-and-weighting.qmd#sec-sampling) and
  [Augmentation](09-augmentation.qmd#sec-augmentation).

Prerequisites: probability and expectation, least squares and logistic regression, and enough
Python to read the code. What to optimize is the subject of
[loss-functions-lab](https://ioannisantoniadis.github.io/loss-functions-lab/), and how to
optimize the subject of [optimization-lab](https://ioannisantoniadis.github.io/optimization-lab/);
this book covers what the model is optimized *on*.

## Connections
